title: Contact — Libriant
metaDescription: Ask before you apply: write to info@libriant.com and we answer within two working days. A screen-share walkthrough, and a written review of your catalogue file.
lede: You do not have to apply in order to ask a question. Write to us with whatever you need to know — the reply comes from the person who builds Libriant, not from an autoresponder.

sections.heading: When you will hear back
body: We answer every message within two working days. If your question needs work at our end — reading through a file of yours, for instance — then within those two days you will at least know when the full answer is coming.
If three working days pass and nothing has arrived, check your spam folder and write again. No question is left unanswered on purpose.

sections.heading: Where to write
sections.intro: There are two addresses, and the same person reads both.

items.title: info@libriant.com
items.body: Anything to do with Libriant: what it does and what it does not do yet, which plan suits the size of your library, how migration from your current system works, a request for a screen-share walkthrough or for a written description of the service.

items.title: privacy@libriant.com
items.body: Anything to do with data protection: access to, correction of or deletion of the details you gave us on the form, withdrawal of your application, or questions about where your members’ data sits and who is able to see it.

sections.footnote: There is no call centre and no service desk with opening hours — these two addresses are all there is. If we need to talk, we arrange a call by email.

sections.heading: Ask before you apply
body: An application is not a precondition for getting an answer. If you would rather first find out whether your collection fits inside a plan, exactly what carries over from your current system, or what Libriant does not do yet, ask us directly.

We will answer even when the answer does not suit us. If what you need is a public catalogue your readers can search for themselves, we will tell you that Libriant does not have one today — and where else to look.

sections.heading: See it working
body: There is no public trial version, and we will not send you to one that does not exist. Instead we arrange a short screen-share session, 20–30 minutes, on whichever tool suits your library.

Tell us beforehand what you want to see and we will have it ready: cataloguing a title by ISBN and by hand, a loan and a return, a hold and the hold queue, custom fields of your own, an export of everything. If you send us a sample of your catalogue first, we show it with your own books rather than with test records.

sections.heading: Send us your file
body: The surest way to find out whether a migration will work is for us to see what you have. Send us a sample — a CSV, an Excel sheet, an export from ABEKT or Koha, MARC as .mrc or MARCXML — and you get a written answer: what is recognised, which column maps to which field, what will need work by hand, and what does not carry over at all.

A few hundred rows are enough; we do not need the whole catalogue. If the file also holds member details, send us the bibliographic part without them — we do not need to see personal data to tell you what will carry over.

If the Greek or the accented characters come out garbled when you open the file, send it exactly as it is. Alongside UTF-8 we also read Windows-1253, the old Greek code page, so a catalogue that mixes Greek and English is the ordinary case here rather than the awkward one.

sections.heading: For schools, colleges and public bodies
body: If you have to put this to a head teacher, a director, a bursar or a committee, ask us for a written description of the service. We send it in everyday language, without technical jargon, in a form that goes into a file: what Libriant does, what it does not do yet, where the data sits, who is able to see it, what applies during the twelve months of the launch offer, and what you decide at the end of them.

During the offer you pay nothing and you sign no supply agreement: we ask for no card and there is no automatic renewal. Before you register your first member we sign a Data Processing Agreement, so that your institution has in writing exactly what we are permitted to do with your members’ data.

If your management wants to know now what will apply in the second year, the plans and the prices are written out at libriant.com/en/pricing. The full commercial and pricing details reach you in writing before any charge.

sections.heading: Requests about your own personal data
body: If you have sent us an application and you want to see, correct or delete what we hold, write to privacy@libriant.com. We answer within 30 days, as the GDPR requires, and you do not have to give a reason. Deletion takes the application with it, and you hear nothing further from us.

For the data of your library’s members the position is a different one: your library is the controller and we are the processor acting on its behalf. If one of your members comes to us, we refer them back to you and give you whatever you need in order to answer them.
Exactly what we keep from the application form, and for how long, is set out in the Privacy Policy at libriant.com/en/privacy.

sections.heading: When you are ready to apply
body: The form is at the foot of the home page, at libriant.com/en/#apply. It asks for the name, type and city of the library, a rough estimate of how many titles you hold, what you use today, and a way to reply to you.
We answer every application within two working days, yes or no. And if you still have questions, send those first — the order does not matter.

title: Who we are — Libriant
metaDescription: Libriant is built by one person, under the name CyberSystema. Who builds it, what does not exist yet, and why your data leaves with you whenever you want.
lede: Behind the “we” on this site there is one person. This page says who that is, what exists today and what does not exist yet — so that you know before you decide, and not in your third month.

sections.heading: Who builds Libriant
body: Libriant is built by one person. That person’s full name and city are printed in the footer of every page on this site and in the Privacy Policy, as the data controller — not hidden behind a contact form.

The same person writes the code, answers your messages, looks at your catalogue file, and signs the Data Processing Agreement that we put in place before you register your first member. It is one person in all four cases.

Everywhere else on this site you will read “we”. We keep it, because commitments are written in the plural — and behind them there is someone with a name. It does not mean departments, shifts and a second office.
We say it at the top of this page rather than at the bottom, because you would have worked it out in the first week of working together anyway.

sections.heading: Why it was built
body: A small or medium-sized library — a school, a college, an institute, a cultural foundation — usually has three roads open to it: a spreadsheet that grows until nobody can manage it, a card file, or a system whose price it cannot see until it asks for it.

Libriant was built for the first two. For the library that knows exactly what it is missing — a clear answer to who has which book and when it comes back — and has neither a budget nor an IT department behind it.

Two decisions came out of that, and they do not change. The first: prices are written on this site, so you do not have to request a quotation to find out what it costs. The second: your data downloads in full at the press of a button, from the first day and on every plan — including the free one.

And a third, technical one. Libriant works in English and in Greek equally, and it reads files saved in Windows-1253, the old Greek code page. If your library is in Greece or Cyprus, part of your catalogue is almost certainly in Greek — donated stock, local publications, a file a predecessor started — and a migration that does not take the old code page into account leaves mangled Greek behind it.

sections.heading: Under the name CyberSystema
body: The software is developed under the name CyberSystema. You will see the name in the footer of the application and in the Privacy Policy.

It is the name the software is written under, and nothing larger than the person described above. It hides no organisation with departments, no investors and no second office. Libriant is the service your library will use, and CyberSystema is the name it is built under.

Everything your finance office needs in writing — the full details for payment, together with the service agreement — reaches you before any charge is made, so that it can be checked at their own pace. At this moment nothing is being charged at all: during the launch offer you pay nothing and sign no procurement, so none of the above is needed in order to start.

sections.heading: What we do not have yet
sections.intro: A list of things you would expect to see on a site like this one and will not find here. They are missing because they do not exist, not because they did not fit.

items.title: Libraries using it
items.body: None yet. Libriant has not gone live in a library, and the five founding places exist for exactly that reason. If anywhere on this site you come across a number of libraries using it, that is a mistake and we would like you to tell us.

items.title: References and testimonials
items.body: There are none, because there is nobody yet to give them. You will not find quoted lines from librarians, nor a row of council logos at the foot of the home page.

items.title: Case studies
items.body: Nor any text along the lines of “how library X cut 40% off the time spent at the circulation desk”. Everything this site says about what Libriant does comes from the software itself, not from measurements in real use that have not been made.

items.title: Awards, funding, partnerships
items.body: None of the three. Libriant has no investors and is not being developed together with any institution. That is not necessarily a drawback, but we will not present it as an advantage.

items.title: A call centre and a guaranteed response time
items.body: Neither exists, and we do not sell tiers of support: no plan buys a faster answer. What does exist is two email addresses, step-by-step help inside the application, a reply to every message within two working days, and availability and support terms agreed with you in writing before you start.

sections.footnote: Whatever the software itself does not do yet is written on the [Features](/en/features) page, in the section “What it does not do yet”. There is no second list that we keep for internal use.

sections.heading: And if you disappear?
body: It is the right question, and we put it before your management does. Libriant is new and one person builds it. That is a real risk and we will not tell you otherwise — an organisation of thirty people would give you a different answer at this point, and we do not have it.
What we can do is not to reduce the probability to zero. It is to make sure that, if it happens, you lose nothing.

A staff seat with the Admin role starts an export from inside the application, without asking us, without a support request and without a notice period. There is no plan that blocks it: it holds on the free Starter plan too, from the first day. The formats are four — CSV, Excel, JSON and SQL, that is, a complete copy of your library’s PostgreSQL database.

The last one is the answer that actually matters. The SQL copy does not depend on us in order to be read: it restores onto any PostgreSQL server, by any technician, with no permission and no key from our side. If you keep a recent copy, the worst case for your library is that it changes system. Unwelcome, but not the same as losing its catalogue.

Two things we will not promise, because they do not exist. There is no deposit of the source code with a third party, and there is no continuity plan guaranteed by somebody else; Libriant is not open-source software and the code is not handed over. The commitment is about your data, not about the software: the data leaves with you, in full, whenever you decide.
The same question is worth putting everywhere. The answer that counts is not how many years someone has been around, but on what terms your data leaves on the day you want to leave.
sections.footnote: The export does not produce MARC. MARC is read on import; it is not written on export. If you need MARC for a reason of your own, tell us before you decide.

sections.heading: One person, not a call centre
sections.intro: That there is one person behind Libriant has two sides, and both of them concern you. We write both, because you will live the second column either way.
columns: What it means on the good days
What it means on the hard days
rows: Whoever answers you has written the piece of code you are asking about. There is no first line of support reading out prepared answers, and no forwarding of your request to another department.
When that person is ill or away, there is nobody else to answer at the same time. That is why we say two working days and not two hours.
A correction your library needs can be in the system within the same week, without passing through a prioritisation committee.

A large new capability takes longer than it would with a team of ten. The public catalogue for your readers is the obvious example: it is on the roadmap, it does not exist today, and we will not charge you for it as though it did.
You know who you are talking to, and it is not a different person with every message. Your library does not have to explain its history from the beginning each time.
There is no support around the clock and we will not pretend that there is. Nor is there a telephone line with service hours; if we need to talk, we arrange a call by email.

sections.heading: How we work
sections.intro: Six rules that hold from the first line of code to this page.

items.title: First it exists, then it gets written
items.body: Everything you read on this site already exists in the software and has a screen inside the application. When something is on the roadmap, we write it as a plan and it does not go into a plan comparison table. We do not charge for a capability that nobody can reach.

items.title: The first libraries set the order
items.body: What gets built next will be decided by the five founding libraries, out of what they find missing in their daily work. There is no investor setting a different order of priorities, and no reason for us to pretend we know better than a circulation desk.

items.title: Every change goes through checks
items.body: The code passes automated checks before it reaches a library, in the same order every time. What exactly they cover is described on the [Security and data protection](/en/security) page. We do not rely on someone remembering to check.

items.title: The migration is ours to do
items.body: For the five founding libraries, moving the catalogue, the members and the open loans across from your current system is our work. You send us your file as it is, without cleaning it up first; we run a trial and show you what will go in and which rows have a problem, before anything is written.

items.title: Greek and English, equally
items.body: There is no main language with a translation trailing behind it. An automated check fails when a piece of text exists in one language and is missing from the other, so that neither of the two falls behind; the language is set per staff seat, not per library.

items.title: We say no as well
items.body: If what your library needs is something Libriant does not do, you will hear it from us before you apply — even when the answer does not suit us. A library that starts with the wrong expectation costs both sides more than an application that was never made.

sections.heading: Why we start with five libraries
body: The number is not a scarcity trick. It is how many migrations one person can do properly within a few months, when each one means looking at your file, matching your columns, running a trial, sending back the rows with problems and going through them again with you.

Five libraries using the system every day tell us more than 50 accounts that open, get tried for a week and are forgotten. And five is few enough that we can answer each one as though it were the only one — because in practice it will be.

Places are given in order of application, and we answer every application within two working days, yes or no. If they fill up before you get there, nothing closes except the offer: Libriant stays available on its normal plans, from the free Starter plan, which covers a whole school library, up to the subscription plans, which start at €390 a year.

sections.heading: What “founding library” means
sections.intro: The term appears in several places on this site, so let it be defined precisely. A founding library is each of the first five libraries to go live with Libriant. What it means in practice:

items.title: The Municipal plan for twelve months, at no charge
items.body: No card details, no automatic renewal and no payment paperwork, because there is no charge. Municipal is the €790 a year plan, with room for 60,000 titles and 25 staff seats. It does not mean that from the second year you pay that amount: at the end of the year you choose the plan that fits the size of your library, and the subscription plans start at €390 a year.

items.title: Moving your files is our work
items.body: The catalogue, the members, the open loans, the holds and the fines are moved by us, not by you. It is not handed to your library as a job it has to find the time to do.

items.title: A permanent discount from the second year
items.body: The five keep a discount that does not expire, on whichever plan they choose. The exact percentage is agreed with you in writing before the first charge. We do not write it here as a number, because it has not yet applied to a single subscription and we do not want you to read it as settled.

items.title: A direct line
items.body: You write straight to the person who builds Libriant, with no step in between. That holds for every library; for the first five it also means that your view sets the order in which the next things get built.

items.title: What we do not ask for in return
items.body: Nothing binding. We do not ask for a public statement, we do not use your library’s name in promotional material without your written permission, and we publish nothing about you. If at some point you want to tell us what could be done better, we will listen carefully — but it is not a condition.

items.title: Leave whenever you want
items.body: With no notice and no penalty, taking all of your data with you first. Being a founding library is not a commitment; it is priority of place and a permanent discount.

sections.footnote: The full terms are on the [Offer terms](/en/offer-terms) page. If anything there looks unclear to you, ask us and we will fix it.

sections.heading: Before you decide
body: If this page made you hesitate, it did its job. We would rather have a library that starts out knowing what is missing than a library that discovers it in the third month.

Ask us at info@libriant.com whatever was not answered here; you do not have to apply in order to get an answer. There is no public trial version: if you want to see the system working, we arrange a short meeting with a shared screen. And if you want to know whether the migration will succeed, send us a sample of your file and we will answer you in writing.
The application form is at the foot of the [home page](/en/#apply). We answer every application within two working days.
