sections.heading: In every plan, without exception — including the free one
sections.intro: What follows is not an add-on and is not locked behind a more expensive plan. It is there from the first day, in the free Starter too.

items.title: Catalogue, lending and members
items.body: Titles and copies on the catalogue, loans, returns, renewals, fines and the member register. The core of the work is not a paid add-on on any plan.

items.title: Details filled in from the ISBN
items.body: Scan or type the ISBN and the edition details come in from OpenLibrary. Plenty of titles are not there — Greek ones especially — so entering a record by hand is an equal path, not a fallback.

items.title: English and Greek
items.body: The whole application in both languages, switched per member of staff. This is not a surface translation: the messages, the labels and the notices are written in both.

items.title: Your own logo and colour
items.body: The screen your staff look at all day resembles your library, not Libriant.

items.title: Export all of your data, whenever you want
items.body: One button downloads your library’s whole database: CSV, Excel, JSON, or a full PostgreSQL dump that restores exactly as it stands. Without asking us, without a request, without a notice period. The export does not include MARC.

items.title: A separate database for each library
items.body: Your data does not sit in a shared table beside other libraries. Each library has a database of its own, and that isolation is tested automatically on every change to the code.

items.title: Data in the European Union
items.body: Hosted inside the EU, with nightly backups.

items.title: Activity log
items.body: Who changed what in members, loans and settings, with the before and the after. You read it yourself; you do not have to ask us for it.

items.title: Support through a one-time code that you issue
items.body: Nobody on this side sees your data without a one-time code that you generate. The access expires after four hours, you can end it whenever you want, and every action we take is recorded and marked as done through Libriant support.

items.title: A Data Processing Agreement before you register your first member
items.body: For your members’ data you are the controller and we are the processor. We sign it before the first member goes into the system, not after.

sections.heading: How the limits are counted
sections.intro: The tables above give you numbers. Here is what they mean in practice, before you show them to whoever is going to ask.

items.title: Titles, not copies
items.body: Titles count, copies do not. Ten copies of the same book are one title.

items.title: Archived titles
items.body: Archived titles do not count. Whatever you take out of circulation stops pressing against the limit, without being deleted.

items.title: Archived members
items.body: Archived members do not count — their loan history stays where it is.

items.title: Staff seats
items.body: Staff seats do not decide your plan: there are three on the free Starter and ten on Community, and deactivated accounts do not hold a seat. What decides the plan is titles.

items.title: Custom fields, per record type
items.body: Custom fields are counted per record type. There are six types: book, copy, member, loan, hold, fine. On Starter the five fields apply to each type separately, not five in total.

items.title: If you reach a limit
items.body: Nothing you already have is deleted or hidden. You simply cannot add new titles or members until you upgrade. “Plan & billing” shows you at any moment how close you are.

items.title: Prices and charging
items.body: Prices are in euros and written by the year, because a Greek library awards its contract by the year. Every plan with a subscription can also be paid monthly; twelve monthly payments cost two months more than the annual price. Nothing is being charged at present. Before the first charge you will have the full commercial details and the billing terms in writing, so your finance office can go through them in its own time.

sections.heading: On-prem / Enterprise
body: Do you need Libriant on your own servers, or are you a size that does not fit the table above? The limits are set case by case and the cost is agreed between us.
We do not write a price here because it would not be a true one: it depends on what runs where, who maintains the server, and what each side takes on. Tell us what you need.

sections.heading: For your finance office
sections.intro: You pay nothing and you sign no procurement contract. We do not ask for a card, there is no automatic renewal, and at the end of the twelve months you decide. Because nothing is charged, you do not need a committed budget line or an award decision to begin. For the moment you do put it in the budget, there are documents — ask and we send them to you.

items.title: A written quotation with a cost breakdown
items.body: What the plan includes, what it costs a year and what it costs a month, and what is not included. The annual figure comes first, because that is the one that goes into the award decision.

items.title: A technical description of the service
items.body: What the software does, where the data is hosted, which roles exist and how data is exported — in a form that goes into a proposal without having to be rewritten.

items.title: Annual payment, with two months free
items.body: Paying once a year is the standard and it is the cheaper one: ten months instead of twelve, so €390 instead of €468 on Community and €790 instead of €948 on Municipal. One expense a year, not twelve. If your office pays monthly instead, that works too.

items.title: A Data Processing Agreement
items.body: You are the controller, we are the processor. Signed before you register your first member.

items.title: A service agreement
items.body: The availability and support terms are agreed with you in writing before you start.

sections.footnote: The commercial documents are issued before any charge, never after. From the second year onwards the relationship becomes an ordinary commercial one, with every document your office requires — and you will have them in hand before you decide. Send a request to info@libriant.com with the subject “Request for a written quotation”.

items.title: Do we have to ask for a quotation to learn the price?
items.body: No. The price is written here: free, €390, €790, €1,190 or €1,890 a year, with the limits next to it. If your office pays monthly, the same plans are €39, €79, €119 and €189 a month. You know what it costs before you speak to us, and you can print it and show it to your management without having asked anyone for anything.

items.title: Do copies count, or titles?
items.body: Titles. Ten copies of the same book are one title. Archived titles and archived members do not count at all, and deactivated staff accounts do not hold a seat. A library with 4,000 titles across 12,000 copies fits entirely inside the free Starter; a library with 18,000 titles across 45,000 copies fits inside Community.

items.title: What happens if we go past a limit?
items.body: Nothing you already have is deleted or hidden. You simply cannot add new titles or members until you upgrade. “Plan & billing” shows you at any moment how close you are to the limits of your plan.

items.title: Why pay, when ABEKT is free?
items.body: ABEKT is the software many Greek libraries have run for years, and the comparison no longer holds in that form. ABEKT 5.6 is no longer distributed — abekt.gr says so itself. Its successor, openABEKT, is a service with an annual subscription, and you learn the price after you ask. So the choice is not between free and paid; it is between a price you cannot see and a price written on this page. And for a great many Greek libraries our price is nothing at all: Starter gives you 5,000 titles, 1,500 members and three staff accounts, free and with no expiry date. A typical Greek school library holds 2,000 to 6,000 items — fewer titles again, since copies do not count — and is kept by one or two people. It fits inside the free plan whole: catalogue, lending and the member register, with nothing to pay and no 14-day trial. You start paying when your collection grows past that size, not before. One more thing, so you do not lose time over it: if what you need is a public catalogue for readers at national level, openABEKT is the right answer and we will tell you so plainly. Libriant is the tool for the staff.

items.title: We already have a catalogue in a file. Do we have to type it in again from the beginning?
items.body: No. Bulk import from CSV, Excel or MARC is in every plan with a subscription, from Community at €390 a year upwards, and you run it yourself from your library’s settings. Before anything is written you run a dry run and see exactly what will go in and which rows have a problem. On the free Starter, bulk import is not included: there you generate a support code, send it to us, and we run the migration. Either way, send us your file first — we look at it and tell you what is in it and what would come across cleanly.

items.title: Can we change plan later on?
items.body: Yes. You change plan from “Plan & billing” and it takes effect straight away — nothing is lost, nothing has to be moved and nothing has to be set up again. If you are between two plans, start with the smaller one and move up when you need to.

items.title: What happens at the end of the twelve months?
items.body: You are never charged automatically. There is no card in the system, so there is nothing that could be charged. A month before the end we get in touch and you choose: either you carry on with a plan of your choosing, with the permanent discount the founding libraries keep, or you stop, download the whole of your data and leave — no questions and no notice period. If you do not reply to us at all, the account stops being active; it does not turn itself into a paid subscription.

items.title: If we leave, do we take our data with us?
items.body: All of it, whenever you want, without asking us. One button downloads your library’s database as CSV, Excel, JSON or a full PostgreSQL dump that restores exactly as it stands. It is in every plan, including the free one, from the first day — it is not the privilege of an expensive plan and it does not pass through us. One clarification so it does not catch you out: the export does not produce MARC. We read MARC on import; we do not write it on export.

items.title: Does it work out cheaper to pay once a year?
items.body: Yes. The annual price is ten months instead of twelve — two months free: €390 instead of €468, €790 instead of €948, €1,190 instead of €1,428, €1,890 instead of €2,268. That is why the annual figure is the one we write first: it is the number that goes into the award decision. And one payment a year means one expense to approve and one line in the budget rather than twelve, which is how a municipality or a school closes its year in any case. If monthly payment suits you better, it stays available on every plan with a subscription.

sections.heading: Five places, twelve months, no charge
body: If your library matches one of the rows above, the application is short and commits you to nothing. We reply to every application within two working days.

If you would rather ask before you apply, write to us at info@libriant.com. Send the file of your current catalogue as well, if you have it to hand — that is where the most useful conversation starts.

title: Security and data protection — Libriant
metaDescription: Where your library’s data is kept, who can see it and under what conditions, what gets recorded, and how you download all of it whenever you want.
lede: This page is written to be forwarded as it stands to your IT department or to your institution’s data protection officer. It describes what is true today — and where something does not exist yet, or needs a step through us, it says so.

sections.heading: The summary, in five lines
body: Your library’s data is kept on servers inside the European Union.
Every library has its own separate database — not shared tables with a column marking which row belongs to whom.
Nobody on our side enters your library without a one-time code that you create; the access expires after four hours and you end it whenever you want.
Under the GDPR you are the controller; we are the processor, and we work on your instructions.
You download your entire database whenever you want, without asking us, on every plan — including the free one.

sections.heading: Where your data lives
body: The servers that run the application, and the libraries’ databases, are inside the European Union.

We do not name a specific country or hosting provider here. Not because it is a secret, but because it is the kind of detail that ought to bind: the exact location, the provider and every other organisation involved in the processing are recorded in the Data Processing Agreement and in the accompanying list of sub-processors, which you receive before you start. A web page changes without you noticing; a signed annex does not.
If your IT department needs those details earlier, for its own assessment, ask and we send them in writing.
The site you are reading right now is separate infrastructure from the application and has no access to any library’s data.

sections.heading: A separate database for every library
body: The usual way to build a service like this is to put every organisation into shared tables and tell them apart with a column. Isolation then rests on whether every query, everywhere in the code, remembered to apply the right filter.

Libriant does not work that way. When a library is created, its own PostgreSQL database is created with it, with its own schema and its own connection address. One library’s catalogue, members, loans, holds, fines and activity log are never in the same tables as another library’s data.

We are not asking you to take that on trust. An automated check runs against a real database on every change to the code: it sets up two libraries from scratch, catalogues a book in the first, then confirms three things. That the second library is refused access when it asks for the first one’s address. That its own catalogue stays empty — the first library’s record appears nowhere. And that a request with no session gets an authentication challenge instead of data. If that check fails, the change does not ship.
The same principle holds at the end of the relationship: when a library closes, its database is deleted in full, not marked inactive.

sections.heading: Who on our side can see your data
sections.intro: The usual answer to this question is vague. Here is a procedure with steps, and every step is started or stopped by you — together with what it does not cover.

items.title: By default, nobody
items.body: There is no screen on our side that opens your catalogue, your members or your loans. Seeing or changing anything inside your library requires the steps that follow, and they all begin with you.

items.title: You create the code
items.body: From your library’s settings, an account with the Admin role generates a one-time code. It is shown exactly once and is not stored anywhere in readable form, not even in our own logs. It is valid for one hour and, as long as it has not been used, you revoke it with one click.

items.title: It is used once, with a second factor
items.body: The code is redeemed exactly once, and only together with two-factor authentication on our side. If two attempts are made at the same moment, one goes through and the other is refused: a single code cannot open two sessions.

items.title: The access lasts four hours
items.body: The session expires on its own four hours after it opens, and is never extended quietly. Carrying on requires a new code — which means a fresh decision by you.

items.title: You end it whenever you want
items.body: A button on your own screen closes the session immediately. The next request from our side is refused. You do not need to tell us, and you do not need to wait.

items.title: You see what happened
items.body: Every request inside the session is recorded with time, method, path and result, and appears on that same screen — live or after the fact. Changes that the activity log covers are marked there as “via Libriant support”, so they can never be confused with something your staff did.

items.title: Two things we do not do inside a support session
items.body: We do not change your plan or your subscription, and we do not delete your library; both require you to act from your own account. That is a commitment, not a technical barrier, and we write it that way because that is what it is. Which is exactly why it matters that every action inside the session is recorded and visible to you.

items.title: What this procedure does not cover
items.body: It covers entry into your library through the application. It does not abolish the obvious: somebody maintains the servers and the databases, and at that level access exists — as it does with any hosted service. The admin panel also has the ability to export a library’s database, restricted to the top-level administrative account. We will not tell you it is technically impossible. We will tell you that every entry into your library goes through the steps above, and that this ability is not used to look at your data.

sections.heading: Backups
body: We take daily backups: the libraries’ databases and the files you upload — covers, member photos, attachments.

The job is built to stop with an error rather than produce a backup that merely looks successful. It verifies that the file it produced decompresses correctly before keeping it. If the folder holding uploaded files is missing, it stops rather than backing up the databases alone. And if a library’s database has been moved to another server, it stops rather than skipping it quietly.

A backup that stays on the same server as the data does not protect against much, so it is copied off that server as well — and if that setting is missing, a warning is logged on every run instead of passing unnoticed. There is a reverse procedure too, written alongside the first: restoring a particular day, databases and files.
Beyond that we do not publish recovery times, availability percentages or guarantees. Availability and support terms are agreed with you in writing before you start; that is where commitments belong.
Your own independent copy you take whenever you want with the data export, further down this page.

sections.heading: Who sees what inside your library
sections.intro: It is your staff who sign in to Libriant. There is no member sign-in and no public catalogue, so there is no public screen standing in front of your members’ data. Inside the library, permissions are set by three roles.
rows: Admin
Library settings, staff seats, subscription, data export, generating and revoking the support code — and all of the day-to-day work.
Librarian
Catalogue, members, loans, returns, renewals, holds, fines. No access to settings, to staff or to the subscription.
Volunteer
Sees the records, does not change them. The role exists for exactly that: so somebody can help without being able to do damage.
sections.footnote: The account that created the library holds the Admin permissions and is the contact for the subscription. Every person gets their own account — shared accounts make the activity log meaningless. An account that is no longer needed is deactivated by an Admin; it then cannot sign in and no longer counts towards your plan’s staff-seat limit.

sections.heading: Activity log
body: The activity log shows who did what and when, with the before and after of the change.
Today it covers: creating, updating, changing the status of and archiving a member; lending, returning, renewing and marking a copy lost; and changes to the library’s settings.

It does not yet cover additions and corrections to the catalogue. We write that out plainly because the difference counts in an audit: if a title or a call number is changed today, you will not find it there. It is planned, and we will not present it to you as though it already exists.
Entries are not deleted after any period and are not limited by your plan. Nowhere does the application offer a way to edit or delete an entry in the log.
Anything done inside a support session carries the marking “via Libriant support”.

sections.heading: GDPR: who is responsible for what
body: The controller is your library, or the institution it belongs to. You decide which member details are collected, for what purpose and for how long.
The processor is us. We process your members’ data in order to run the service, and on your instructions — not for purposes of our own.

That relationship is set out in a Data Processing Agreement under Article 28 of the GDPR, together with the list of organisations involved as sub-processors. The text is not published yet: it is with legal review and will be provided when it is ready. We will not ask you to enter the details of a single member before you have it in your hands, signed.

Nowhere do we write that we are “GDPR compliant”. Compliance is not a stamp collected once; it is documented, reviewed again, and part of it is your own responsibility as controller. What we can state is specific things, such as the ones described on this page.

We hold no ISO or SOC certification and will not claim that we do. If your institution requires such a certification from the service it chooses, tell us early: it is a criterion we do not meet today.

sections.heading: Your members’ rights, in practice
sections.intro: Requests from members come to you, as the controller. Here is what you do from inside the application, and where a step through us is needed.

items.title: Access and portability
items.body: A member’s record and their loan history are visible on their card and are included in the data export, in formats that open anywhere. There is nothing you need to ask us for.

items.title: Rectification
items.body: Every field of the record can be corrected by staff with the Librarian or Admin role. The correction is recorded in the activity log with the before and after, so when it was made and by whom is documented.

items.title: Erasing a member’s details
items.body: This one needs care, so we say it before you meet it. What the application offers today is archiving a member, not permanent deletion from the screen: an archived member drops out of the working lists and no longer counts towards your plan’s limits, but the record remains. For permanent erasure of a particular member’s details, send us a request and we carry it out.

items.title: Deleting the whole library
items.body: Done at your written request. The action requires the library’s exact identifier to be typed as confirmation, deletes its database and its files, and is recorded. It cannot be undone — download your export first. Backups already taken hold a trace for a limited period, which is set out in the Data Processing Agreement.

items.title: Members who are minors
items.body: In school libraries, and in the children’s section of a community library, many members are under 18. The legal basis, and informing parents or guardians, are your responsibility as controller. On our side, the service does not ask for and does not need special categories of data in order to work; if you choose to add such data in fields of your own, that is on your responsibility and it is best to tell us.

items.title: No other use
items.body: We do not use your members’ data for any other purpose. We do not sell it, we do not release it for advertising, we do not build profiles, and we do not train artificial-intelligence models on it.

sections.heading: You take your data whenever you want
body: An account with the Admin role starts an export from inside the application. There is no request to us, no notice period, and no plan that blocks it: it works on the free Starter plan too.

Four formats, depending on what you want to do. CSV for spreadsheets, Excel, JSON for moving into another system, and SQL — a full copy of your library’s PostgreSQL database, which restores as it is onto a server of your own.
The download link is valid for 24 hours. After that you ask for a fresh export; nothing is lost.

This is also the substantive answer to the question your management will put to you: “and what if they stop?”. The SQL copy does not need us in order to be read. It is an ordinary PostgreSQL database, and any technician can restore it.
sections.footnote: The export does not produce MARC. MARC is supported on import, not on export. If you need MARC for a reason of your own, tell us before you decide.

sections.heading: This site does not track you
body: No analytics, no tracking cookies, no third-party fonts, no social-network code. That is why you saw no consent window: there is nothing for us to ask your consent about.

Do not take that on trust — check it. View the page source, or open your browser’s developer tools on the network tab and reload: you will see this site’s own files and, if the form protection is switched on, the one script described just below.

The single exception concerns protecting the application form from automated submissions. When it is switched on, one script loads for exactly that purpose — the only request to an outside server anywhere on this site. The network provider in front of the site may also set a strictly necessary bot-protection cookie lasting half an hour. It does not count visits and does not follow you elsewhere. Both are described in detail in the Privacy Policy.
In the application there is a session cookie, because without it there is no signing in. There is no advertising or analytics cookie there either.

sections.heading: How the software is built and how it is checked
sections.intro: Every change to the code goes through the same sequence of checks before it reaches a library. It is the same sequence for day-to-day development, for release to production and for the desktop app build — one definition, so that no route can skip a check that another route runs.

items.title: Static checks
items.body: Type checking across the whole codebase, style and formatting checks, and a check that the application’s English and Greek texts are in full correspondence, so that neither of the two languages falls behind.

items.title: Over 300 automated tests
items.body: They cover the logic behind the screens: plan limits, role permissions, fine calculation, the hold queue, validation of your own fields, handling of charges.

items.title: Tests against a real database
items.body: Eight scenarios run against real PostgreSQL, not a simulation: a full library flow from the catalogue through to the return, file import, role permissions, desktop app access, and the isolation between libraries described above.

items.title: Testing the schema changes
items.body: Changes to the structure of the database are applied to a clean database on every run, so that an upgrade never runs for the first time on your data.

items.title: A security review before release
items.body: The system went through a systematic security and reliability review before it was offered to a library. The findings were recorded one by one and dealt with. It was an internal review, not certification by an independent body, and we do not present it as one.

items.title: What this does not guarantee
items.body: That there will never be a bug. No process guarantees that. It guarantees that bugs are caught early, and that we do not rely on somebody remembering to check.

items.title: Is there an API so we can connect it to other systems?
items.body: No. There is no programming interface, and we will not tell you otherwise in order to get through an evaluation. Exchanging data today is done by importing and exporting files, and both directions are in your hands.

items.title: Does anything need installing on staff computers?
items.body: No. Libriant works in the browser. There is also a desktop app on the plans with a subscription, for silent printing of loan receipts and labels without a dialogue box — it is an option, not a prerequisite.

items.title: Can we install it on our own servers?
items.body: Yes, by arrangement. The limits are set case by case and pricing is agreed. Tell us what your institution requires.

items.title: Do readers have access?
items.body: No. There is no member sign-in and no public catalogue. It is your staff who sign in to the application. It is a design choice, and it also narrows the exposed surface: there is no public screen standing in front of your members’ data.

items.title: How does staff sign-in work?
items.body: With a separate account per person and a password, per library. Repeated failed sign-in attempts are throttled automatically. A forgotten password is reset by the Admin from the settings.

items.title: What happens if a member of staff leaves?
items.body: The Admin deactivates the account. They can no longer sign in, their actions stay in the activity log under their name, and the account no longer counts towards your plan’s limit.

sections.heading: If you need something that is not here
body: Write to us. For data protection matters: privacy@libriant.com. For anything else: info@libriant.com. We answer every message within two working days.
If your IT department or your management needs a written technical description of the service to attach to a recommendation, ask and we send it.
Ask before you apply. It is better to find out now that something is not covered than three months later. More ways to get in touch on the Contact page.

title: Migrating from your current system — Libriant
metaDescription: How your catalogue, members and open loans come into Libriant — from ABEKT, Koha, Excel, CSV or MARC, with a dry run that shows what will land before anything is written.
lede: Migration is the reason many libraries stay on the system they have, even when it no longer serves them. Here is what Libriant reads, what transfers, what does not, and what we will need from your library.

sections.heading: We do the migration for you
body: For the first five libraries, we do the migration ourselves. You send us whatever you have — an export from your current system, an Excel sheet, or a file you already know is in a poor state — and we hand your library back set up, together with a report of everything that could not go in and why.
You do not need to clean the file before you send it. Cleaning it is part of the work, not a condition for starting.

If you would rather do it yourself, migration is a feature inside Libriant and you run it from your library’s settings. Bulk file import is included in every plan with a subscription — Community, Municipal and Institutional — and the launch offer gives you Municipal. It is not part of the free Starter plan: if you have a file to bring across and you are considering the free plan, write to us before you decide.

sections.heading: What you can come from
sections.intro: Libriant does not connect to the database of the system you have today. It reads what that system exports, and it accepts five formats: CSV, TSV, Excel (.xlsx), MARC21 in binary form (.mrc) and MARCXML (.xml).

items.title: ABEKT
items.body: If your catalogue lives in ABEKT, as a great many catalogues in Greece do, we need its export rather than its database: whatever it gives you in MARC or in a delimited file can be read. MARC21 tags are recognised automatically — 245$a for the title, 020$a for the ISBN, 100$a for the author. Tags from another MARC variant appear as columns under their own name, and you map them once, for the whole file. If you are not sure which export is the right one, send us a sample and we will tell you.

items.title: Koha or another system
items.body: If the system you have exports CSV or MARC, that is the route. There is no live synchronisation between the two systems and we do not promise you one: the migration happens with a file, at a moment you choose.

items.title: An Excel, CSV or TSV sheet
items.body: .xlsx is read directly, and if the workbook holds several sheets you choose which one. In CSV the separator is detected automatically — comma, semicolon, tab or pipe — because the “CSV” that Excel writes in a Greek or most European locales is usually semicolon-separated. Dates are read in European order, day first, and the order can be switched per column if your file runs the other way.

items.title: MARC (.mrc, .xml)
items.body: MARC21 in ISO 2709 binary form, and MARCXML. Each record becomes one row and each field or subfield one column, so you see your file as a table before you decide what goes across. Repeated fields and subfields are joined into a single cell with a pipe.

items.title: A card file or a notebook
items.body: Here there is no file to migrate, so the question changes: you catalogue by hand inside Libriant, filling in details from the ISBN where there is one, or you first type a sheet with a few columns and we bring it across in bulk. Reckon with this: ISBN lookup draws on OpenLibrary, and a good many Greek titles are not held there — part of the catalogue will be typed by hand. Tell us how many titles there are and we will tell you which of the two routes is less work.

items.title: Your members, wherever they are
items.body: Members are rarely in the same file as the catalogue. They come from a sheet of their own: full name, member number, email, phone, address, joining date. Only the full name is required. Where there is no member number, Libriant assigns one during the import.

sections.heading: What transfers, and in what order
sections.intro: The order is not a recommendation, it is a requirement. A copy cannot go in before its book, nor a loan before its member and its copy. Each file goes across separately, with its own column mapping, in this order. Libriant links records to what it already holds: ISBN or title for the book, barcode for the copy, member number or email for the member.
rows: Authors
Full name. Optionally birth and death years, notes.
Books
Title. Optionally ISBN, publisher, year, language, pages, call number, description, authors.
Copies
A unique code (barcode or accession number) and the book the copy belongs to, by ISBN or title. Optionally shelf location, condition, date acquired, price.
Members
Full name. Optionally member number, email, phone, address, joining date.
Loans
Member number or email, copy barcode and due date. Both open and closed loans go across.
Holds
Member number or email and the book, by ISBN or title.
Fines
Member number or email, amount and reason.
sections.footnote: An open loan comes across with the due date it already had; it does not start again from the beginning. A copy will not take a second open loan: if your file holds two, the second row comes out as an error instead of passing silently. Cover images and attached files do not transfer — the import takes text and numbers. Holds are always placed by staff, in a migration as in daily use.

items.title: Upload
items.body: You say what you are importing — authors, books, copies, members, loans, holds or fines — and upload the file. The format and the character encoding are detected; both can be stated by hand if the detection gets it wrong. The start of the file is read straight away, so that beside each column you see a sample of your own data before you go further. The limits per file are 64 MB and 250,000 rows.

items.title: Map columns
items.body: For each column in your file you choose where it goes. The ones that are recognised arrive already filled in: headings are matched with accents, capitals and punctuation ignored, and Greek headings are recognised as readily as English ones — “τίτλος” as well as “title”, “γραμμωτός κώδικας” as well as “barcode”, “ημερομηνία επιστροφής” as well as “due date” — alongside the MARC21 tags. Anything you do not want to bring across, you leave on “Don’t import”. That is also where a column matching no Libriant field stays: it does not transfer, so if it holds something you need, tell us before you run the import. This is also where you say what happens to records that already exist.

items.title: Review
items.body: You run the dry run. The whole file goes down the same path it would follow in a real import, and at the end nothing is written. You get the report, download the rows that came back with errors, correct what is worth correcting and run it again as many times as you need.

items.title: Done
items.body: You give the command to import. The job runs in the background, with a counter showing how many rows have gone through, and it does not hold you in front of the screen. A row that fails does not bring the file down: the rest go through and that one is recorded with its reason. At the end you see how many records were imported, how many updated and how many skipped.

sections.heading: The dry run: you see what will land, before it lands
body: The dry run is not a check of the file format. It is the real import with writing switched off: every row is read, every value converted, every reference looked up — the book a copy points at, the member and the copy a loan points at — and your plan’s limits are checked as well. Then nothing is written.

The report gives four numbers: how many rows the file holds, how many will import, how many errors, how many warnings. Below them the problems appear one by one, with row number, field and what is wrong: no four-digit year found; the due date is not after the checkout date; no matching book was found for this copy, import the books first.
And you download them: a CSV with one line per problem — row number, field, code, message. You open it beside your file and correct precisely, instead of going through 5,000 rows by eye.
Warnings stop nothing, but they are worth reading: that is where you see, for instance, that a loan marked as returned carried no return date and the current date was used in its place.

If you change the mapping, the previous dry run is discarded, so that you never read a report belonging to a different mapping. And an import that stopped halfway starts again from the beginning: with “Skip it” chosen, the authors, books, copies and members that had already gone through are recognised by their stable keys and skipped, rather than written a second time.

sections.heading: Greek that does not break
body: The files Greek libraries keep are not all in UTF-8. Many are in Windows-1253, the code page of the Greek Windows of the era in which most of these catalogues were built.

Libriant expects that. If the file carries an encoding mark at its start, that mark is respected. Otherwise UTF-8 is tried under a strict check and, if the data is not valid UTF-8, the reader falls back to Windows-1253. This is not a guess weighed by probability: it is a fixed sequence of attempts, and it never ends in a read error. If it does get it wrong, you state the encoding yourself at upload — UTF-8, Windows-1253, Windows-1252 or ISO-8859-7 — and the file is read again.

In practice, you will not find gibberish where you expected “ΑΡΧΑΙΟΛΟΓΙΑ”. And because the sample appears on the very first screen, you see it before you do anything else: if the Greek looks broken there, state the encoding and run it again.

One limit, written here rather than left for you to discover later: if the MARC file is in MARC-8, the older MARC encoding, its structure reads normally — records, fields, subfields — but Greek and accented characters may come out wrong, because MARC-8 is not converted. Modern exports are in UTF-8. If yours is not, ask your system for a UTF-8 export, or take the CSV route instead.

sections.heading: When a record already exists
sections.intro: Before you run, you say what happens when a row matches a record that is already there. The choice applies to the whole file, and its effect shows in the dry run, before it is applied.
rows: Skip it
The row is passed over. The record that exists is left untouched.
On the first migration, and on every repeat after a correction: what has gone through is not written again.
Update it
The record that exists is updated with the values in the row.
When your file is more correct than what has already gone in — a second, cleaner pass.
Report as an error
The row does not go through and is recorded as an error, with the reason.
When you are not expecting duplicates and want to know if there are any.
sections.footnote: Matching is done on fixed criteria, not on a similarity score: an author by normalised name, a book by ISBN-13, a copy by its barcode, a member by member number and, where that is missing, by email. Loans, holds and fines are not checked for duplicates: if you run the same loan file twice, the open loans are stopped by the rule of one open loan per copy, but the closed ones will be written again.

sections.heading: How long it takes
body: We do not give you guaranteed times. We have not put enough catalogues through to claim a number and then keep to it, and a number that is not kept is worse than no number at all.

We do know where the time goes, though, and it does not go on the machine. It goes on mapping the columns, which is done once per record type, and on the second and third dry run, where you look at what came back with errors and decide whether it can be corrected in the file or is better left out.

Plan it as two separate sittings rather than one: the catalogue first, meaning books and copies, and the members with their open loans at a second sitting. The second is worth doing as close as you can to the day you start working in Libriant, so that it is current.
Keep your present system running until you have checked the result. There is no reason to close it the same day, and if something needs running again you will want it open.

If a file goes over 64 MB or 250,000 rows, you split it into parts and run them one after another. With “Skip it” chosen, a part that goes through twice by mistake does not create duplicate books, copies or members.

sections.heading: What we need from your library

items.title: A file, as it is
items.body: An export from your current system, or the sheet you keep. It does not need cleaning first: whatever does not hold up will show in the dry run, with a row number against it.

items.title: Someone who knows what the columns mean
items.body: A few headings do not explain themselves: CODE2, T.A., a column that holds nothing but Y and N — or the same three abbreviated in Greek, in an older file. It takes a member of staff to say what they are, because one wrong decision here is copied across thousands of records.

items.title: A decision about what does not come
items.body: Old loan history, members who have not appeared for years, records for material no longer on the shelf. A migration is the natural moment to leave them behind, and the decision is yours.

items.title: A unique code for every copy
items.body: Each copy needs a code of its own: letters, digits, hyphens, full stops or underscores, up to 64 characters — a barcode or an accession number. Libriant does not invent one on your behalf. If the copies have never been numbered, this is the moment the numbering gets decided.

items.title: Time to check after the import
items.body: Open 20 records at random and compare them with the shelf, and look at two or three members with an open loan. If a column has landed in the wrong field, that is where it shows — and the sooner it shows, the less has been built on top of it.

items.title: A target date
items.body: When you want your library working in Libriant. Without a date, a migration is put off indefinitely; with one, we both know what has to be ready and when.

sections.heading: And if you decide to leave
body: We write this before you ask, because it is a fair question to put to a system with no history behind it: your data comes out whenever you want, without asking our permission and without notice.

Export is not a capability you buy. It is on every plan, the free one included, from the first day. You start it from settings, the file is prepared in the background, and it appears for download when it is ready. It is kept for about a day, and you can ask for it again whenever you like.

There are four formats. CSV: one file per table, inside a zip. Excel (.xlsx): one sheet per table. JSON: for whoever writes the conversion into your next system. SQL: a complete copy of your library’s database, made with pg_dump, without owners and privileges, which restores into any PostgreSQL installation. The last one is not an extract and not a report; it is your database.

One thing the export does not do: it does not produce MARC. MARC is read on the way in, not written on the way out. If your next system requires MARC, a conversion from the CSV will be needed, and Libriant does not hand you that ready-made today. We write it here so that you do not discover it on the day you need it.
Every library has a separate database of its own. What you download is yours, whole.

sections.heading: Send us a sample of your file
body: 20 rows are enough. We look at them and write back telling you what reads, what will take work and what does not transfer at all — before you decide anything, with no application to fill in and no commitment of any kind.
Send it to info@libriant.com, with a line or two about what the file is and which system produced it. We answer every message within two working days.

If the sample is of members, send the headings without real details: the column names are enough for us to understand the structure. Members’ personal data does not need to be seen by us before there is a signed Data Processing Agreement.

title: Which libraries — Libriant
metaDescription: School, community, special, municipal or academic: what a day looks like in each type of library, which plan two numbers give you, and where Libriant does not fit.
lede: The same system runs a school library with 1,200 titles and a municipal one with 30,000. What changes is the limits of the plan, and four capabilities that start to mean something once there is more staff and more material. Below you will find what a day looks like in each type of library, which plan that works out to — and, at the end, which library Libriant does not serve today.

sections.heading: Two misconceptions, up front
body: If you are reading this from a school library of a few thousand titles, looked after by one person between lessons: your library is not too small for Libriant — most likely it fits inside the free plan whole. Starter gives you a catalogue, members and loans for 5,000 titles, 1,500 members and three staff seats. A typical Greek school library holds 2,000 to 6,000 items, and titles are fewer than items because copies of the same book count once — so most school libraries in the country sit inside the free plan and never pay anything. It is not a trial period and it does not expire. We do not ask for card details, and you do not have to talk to anyone to find out what it costs.

If you are reading this from a municipal IT department or from an institution’s management: this is not an experimental tool. Each library has its own separate database, data is hosted inside the European Union, permissions are set by three roles, changes to members, loans and settings are recorded with the before and the after, and your library’s entire database downloads with one button whenever you want. What exactly holds true, together with its limits, is on [Security and data protection](/en/security).

One thing holds in both cases: Libriant is the staff’s tool. There is no public catalogue for readers, and members do not sign in anywhere. If that is what you are looking for, the last section of this page tells you where to look instead.

sections.heading: What is the same, whichever type you are
body: The type of library is declared on the application form and goes onto the library profile. It does not change the screens, it does not unlock or lock features, and it does not set the price. The plan is decided mainly by one number: how many titles your catalogue holds. Members and staff seats are set high enough on every plan that they will not move you up a step.

The core is the same everywhere, including on the free plan: a catalogue of titles and copies, a member register, loans, returns, renewals, fines, detail pre-fill from an ISBN, custom fields of your own, Greek and English, your own logo, an activity log, and export of all your data whenever you want it.

Four things are absent from the free Starter and present in every plan with a subscription: holds with a queue, email notices to members, bulk file import, and the desktop app. Everything else is described in [Features](/en/features), and the limits line by line in [Pricing](/en/pricing).

sections.heading: School library
body: The day is not continuous. The library opens at break, again after the last lesson, and the work is done by one person who also teaches. Loans arrive in bursts, a whole class at once, and the catalogue grows from donations and from an order that lands once a year. The big moment is June, when everything has to come back before the school closes.

Four things from Libriant count here. Barcode scanning with the device camera, where the browser supports it (Firefox does not today), so that the desk is where you are and not where a computer happens to be. Entering records by hand, which is an equal path and not a fallback: ISBN lookup goes to OpenLibrary, and while an English-language edition is usually there, Greek-published school books frequently are not, so the search will come back empty. A custom “class” field on the member record, so that the class a child belongs to sits next to their name. And the list of overdue loans, which in June is the whole of the last week’s work.

The size: the free Starter covers 5,000 titles, 1,500 members and three staff seats, and a typical Greek school library holds 2,000 to 6,000 items — which means fewer titles than items, since copies of the same book count once. A collection of 1,200 titles, for instance, sits comfortably inside it with room to grow for years. Most school libraries in the country will never pay, and that is not an offer; it is how the limit was written. The three seats mean the person who keeps the library can also give a seat to whoever covers for them, without changing plan.

What takes a school library off the free plan is rarely its size. More often it is a school complex cataloguing more than one unit in the same catalogue, or the need for holds with a queue, for bulk import you run yourself, and for the desktop app — three of the four things absent from Starter that matter in a school. The next step up is Community: €390 a year, or €39 a month if monthly billing suits you better, with 20,000 titles, 5,000 members and ten staff seats.

If a catalogue already exists in a spreadsheet: bulk import is not included in the free plan. There you generate a support code, send it to us, and we run the migration. From Community upwards you run it yourself from your library’s settings, after a dry run has first shown you what would go in. The steps are on [Migration](/en/migration).
For schools that teach in English and for foreign-language schools: the whole application exists in both languages, and each staff member chooses their own.

sections.heading: Community library
body: Open certain hours a week, often with volunteers who change shift and who do not all have the same relationship with a computer. The collection grows mostly from donations, so cataloguing happens in batches — a box of books that has to go in at some point. The members are neighbours, and the library answers to an association or to a community that asks where the books went.

Three things from Libriant count here. The Volunteer role, which sees the catalogue, members and loans without changing anything, so that someone can help at the shelves without being able to affect the data. The activity log, which shows who changed what in members, loans and settings — with rotating shifts that is not bureaucracy, it is how a question gets answered without anyone being blamed. And holds with a queue, for the one copy that five people want.

The size: a community library with a few thousand titles and a few hundred members fits inside the free Starter, which runs to 5,000 titles, 1,500 members and three staff seats. Community, €390 a year or €39 a month, starts to be needed once the catalogue passes 5,000 titles, or when you want holds with a queue and bulk import you run yourself; it runs to 20,000 titles, 5,000 members and ten staff seats.

One point worth knowing: each person needs a seat of their own, because shared accounts void the activity log. And anyone who records loans needs the Librarian role — a Volunteer does not lend and does not record a return. That used to carry an unfair cost: seats were few, and a library with six volunteers on shifts was pushed onto a larger plan than its catalogue justified. It was a fair complaint and we have fixed it: the free Starter gives three seats, Community ten and Municipal twenty-five. ELSTAT recorded 1,754 library staff across 338 libraries in 2024 — and since the large libraries are counted in that figure too, the typical one runs on one or two people. How many volunteers you have should not decide your plan, and it no longer does. Seats that are deactivated stop counting towards the limit, so someone who has left does not hold one.

sections.heading: Special library (organisation, foundation, society)
body: The collection is closed and focused: legal, medical, technical, a museum, a foreign cultural institute, a learned society. The members are few and known by name — colleagues at the organisation, perhaps outside researchers by arrangement. Loans are few but long, and the question that hurts is not how many books there are, but where that one book is and who has been holding it for two years.

What counts from Libriant is the library policy, which you set yourself — a 90-day loan period, as many renewals as you allow, a cap on active loans per member or no cap at all — and your own custom fields, because a special collection almost always has an identifier of its own: accession number, its own classification, department, funder. The classification goes on the title, while the barcode and the shelf location go on each copy separately — so that two copies of the same book can sit in different places.
For foreign-language institutes and for organisations with international staff, the switch between Greek and English is per staff member: two people at the same desk can work in different languages.

Size varies here more than in any other category. An association library with 400 titles and one person fits inside the free Starter. A hospital or research-institute library with 20,000 titles and eight staff is Municipal. The rule stays the same: the two numbers, not the label.
If your collection is not mainly books — archival material, maps, museum objects, audiovisual material — read the last section of this page first.

sections.heading: Public or municipal library
body: A clarification first, because it matters: in Greece a Public Library is institutionally a separate category from a municipal one. In Libriant both are recorded under the same type, because the daily work at the desk is the same and because the type changes nothing about how the software behaves. The plans that libraries of both kinds end up on are named Municipal and Central, but neither rules out either kind: size decides, not the name over the door.

The day is not yours to control. Returns in the morning, the children’s section in the afternoon, someone who has lost their card, someone asking for a book that is already out on loan, a school visit nobody announced. The staff are more than one person, with different responsibilities, and the library answers upwards.

Four things from Libriant count here. The hold queue: a member asks for a book that is out and the librarian records the hold on their behalf — members do not place holds themselves, because they do not sign in anywhere. The queue keeps the order of priority and, the moment the copy is returned, the first person is promoted automatically to ready for pickup. The three roles and the activity log, which in a public body are not a luxury. The desktop app, which prints the loan receipt and the copy label straight to the printer, without a print dialogue on every loan. And the overdue list, which in a library with thousands of members is standing work rather than an incident.

One thing is better known now than discovered in use: email notices to members exist as a feature, with texts, switches and a regular check of loans, but no mail sender has been set up yet — so today no message reaches a member. We will update this page when that changes.

The size: Municipal covers 60,000 titles, 15,000 members and twenty-five staff seats, at €790 a year — or €79 a month, if monthly billing suits you better. The median Greek public library holds around 67,000 volumes, which works out at roughly 53,000 titles, so the 60,000-title limit was written for exactly that number: an ordinary library has no business sitting on an institutional plan because it holds the books it is supposed to hold. If the collection is larger, or you run branches, the next step up is Central: 150,000 titles, 40,000 members, sixty staff seats, €1,190 a year. Municipal is also the plan the launch offer gives to the first five libraries, with no charge for twelve months.

For the finance office, a benchmark from public records: we looked at 76 awards for library software published on Diavgeia, the Greek public-spending register. The median Greek library pays around €900 a year, the most common contract is €500, and the range runs from €300 to €1,700. The €790 of Municipal sits inside that range and below the median spend — we are not asking you to change the order of magnitude of your budget in order to change system. Two pages you will most likely need to forward: [Security and data protection](/en/security) for the IT department, and [Pricing](/en/pricing) for the finance office — where it is also explained that, because nothing is charged during the offer, no budget commitment or procurement decision is needed in order to start.

sections.heading: Academic library (university or research body)
body: The load is not steady: the weeks around the start of each semester carry a disproportionate share of the year. Members run into the thousands and turn over every September. The staff are organised, often with students at the desk, and alongside the central library there are department, laboratory and institute libraries holding their own material and their own loans.

Three things from Libriant count here: the limits — 400,000 titles, 100,000 members, 150 staff seats; the roles, so that whoever helps at the shelves can look without changing anything, while whoever records loans holds the Librarian role; and full bilingualism, for departments that teach in English and for students who do not read Greek.

Here we owe you plain speaking. Libriant has no acquisitions, does not track serial issues, does not speak Z39.50 and does not send records to a union catalogue. If your institution’s central library depends on those, Libriant does not replace it, and we will not tell you otherwise.

Where it fits cleanly is the department, laboratory or research-institute library: its own catalogue, its own loans, one to three people, and a collection that today lives in a spreadsheet or in a notebook. That size fits inside the free Starter almost every time, and moves to Community once the catalogue passes 5,000 titles or holds with a queue are needed.

The size: for an institution’s central library, Institutional — 400,000 titles, 100,000 members, 150 staff seats, €1,890 a year or €189 a month. Between Municipal and Institutional there is a step in the middle, Central: 150,000 titles, 40,000 members, sixty staff seats, €1,190 a year. We wrote it for the central municipal or public library with branches, but it also covers the research-body library that is larger than a municipal one and smaller than a university’s central library. For a department or institute library: the free Starter up to 5,000 titles, Community at €390 a year up to 20,000, and Municipal at €790 above that. And if the institution wants Libriant on its own servers, or is a size the table does not hold, the limits and the cost are agreed case by case.
