sections.heading: Where Libriant does not fit today
sections.intro: It is not for every library. We would rather you read this here than discover it after you have moved your catalogue across.

items.title: If what you mainly need is a public catalogue for readers
items.body: There is none. There is no Libriant screen that a reader ever sees: members do not sign in, do not search the catalogue from home, do not renew and do not place holds. If your library is judged on whether the public can find its collection, you need a system that publishes one — for libraries in Greece, openABEKT from the National Documentation Centre is the right answer, and we will tell you so directly. Libriant solves the internal problem: who has which book, and when it comes back.

items.title: If you have to take part in a union or national catalogue
items.body: Z39.50, SRU and OAI-PMH are not supported, so you do not pull a ready-made bibliographic record from another library and you do not send your own outwards. And export does not produce MARC: MARC goes into Libriant, it does not come out. If taking part in a union catalogue is an obligation for your institution, that is an obstacle and not a detail.

items.title: If your collection is not mainly books
items.body: Every record in the catalogue is a book. You do not define material types of your own with their own screens, so archival material, maps, museum objects or audiovisual material have no model of their own. The practical route today is a custom “material type” field on the record: it works for a mixed collection with a few non-book items, it does not work for an archive or a museum.

items.title: If you need acquisitions, serials or a link to other systems
items.body: There is no order management for new material, no issue tracking, and no interface for other software to talk to Libriant. The road out is export — CSV, JSON, Excel and a full PostgreSQL copy that restores exactly as it was — and you have it on every plan, from the first day.

sections.footnote: None of these lines comes with a date, because we will not promise dates. When something changes, this page changes with it. The full list of what Libriant does not do yet is on [Features](/en/features).

sections.heading: If it is not clear where your library belongs
body: Write us two numbers — roughly how many titles your catalogue holds, and how many people will be working in Libriant — and we will tell you which plan that works out to. If the numbers are not known, tell us what kind of library it is and what makes the work hard today; the more useful conversation comes out of that anyway. [Contact](/en/contact) has the addresses.

Send the file of your current catalogue as well, exactly as it is. There is no need to clean it up first — cleaning up is part of the work, not a precondition for starting. We will tell you what transfers and what will need work by hand: [Migration](/en/migration).

If your library is none of the five categories, the type on the form has an “Other” option, and at the end of the form there is a free-text field where you can tell us what it is. [Apply for one of the five places](/en/#apply).

title: Frequently asked questions — Libriant
metaDescription: Answers on the launch offer, the plans, migrating from ABEKT or a spreadsheet, your data and GDPR — and on what Libriant does not do yet.
lede: The questions librarians ask before they switch systems, answered. Where something does not exist yet, you read it here — not after you have found out halfway through a working day.

sections.heading: The offer and the plans
sections.intro: The price and the limits of every plan are written out on the Plans and pricing page. You do not have to request a quote to find out what it costs.

items.title: Why pay, when ABEKT is free?
items.body: The comparison does not hold the way you remember it: ABEKT 5.6 is no longer distributed, as its own page at abekt.gr states. Its successor, openABEKT, is a service with an annual subscription whose price you learn after you request a quote. So the choice is not between free and paid, but between a price you cannot see and a price written down here. And in a great many cases you pay nothing at all: the free Starter plan covers 5,000 titles, 1,500 members and three staff seats. A Greek school library usually holds 2,000 to 6,000 books, and copies of the same title count once — so the whole of it fits, with all of its staff, on no subscription. This is not a 14-day trial, nor a free plan built to be outgrown in the first month: it is the system you will be working in.

items.title: What do the first five libraries get, and what happens after that?
items.body: You get the whole Municipal plan for twelve months — no charge, no card, no automatic renewal — and we move your catalogue across for you. Municipal is the €790 a year plan: 60,000 titles, 15,000 members and 25 staff seats, which covers the median Greek public library. It does not mean you pay that from the second year on: at the end of the twelve months you choose the plan that fits the size of your library. The subscription plans start at €390 a year — or €39 a month, if monthly billing suits you better — and for collections up to 5,000 titles Starter is free. We get in touch a month before the twelve months are up, and founding libraries keep a permanent discount on top of whatever they choose. If you never reply to us at all, the account stops being active — it does not turn itself into a subscription.

items.title: We are a public body — a municipality, a state school, a public college. What do we need in order to start?
items.body: You pay nothing and you sign no procurement contract. We do not ask for a card, there is no automatic renewal, and at the end of the twelve months you decide. Because there is no charge, you do not need a committed budget line or an award decision to begin — and the twelve months give you room to put it into next year’s budget. From the second year on, a normal commercial relationship is needed: before any charge you will receive the full commercial and pricing terms in writing, so your finance office can go through them at its own pace.

items.title: Do titles count, or copies — and what happens if we reach a limit?
items.body: Titles count, not copies: ten copies of the same book are one title. Archived titles and archived members do not count at all, and inactive staff seats do not take up a place. If you reach a limit, nothing you already hold is deleted or hidden — you cannot add new titles or members until you move up a plan. You can see how close you are at any time from Plan & billing, which is also where the plan change happens, and it takes effect immediately.

sections.heading: What Libriant does and does not do

items.title: Is there a public catalogue for readers (OPAC)?
items.body: Not yet. Today Libriant is the staff’s tool. A public catalogue for readers is planned, but it does not exist today and we will not charge you for it as though it did. If what you need first is your collection visible in a national catalogue, openABEKT is the right answer for you. Libriant is for the library whose problem is internal: who has which book, and when it comes back.

items.title: Can members place their own holds?
items.body: No — every hold is entered by staff. The librarian places the hold for the member, the hold queue keeps the order of priority, and as soon as the copy comes back the first person is promoted automatically to ready for pickup. You set how many hours the copy waits on the pickup shelf; if that window passes, the queue moves on to the next person. Holds and the waiting list are available from the Community plan upwards.

items.title: Does it work in English — and will it find our Greek titles from the ISBN?
items.body: The interface is complete in English from the first day, with a switch between English and Greek per staff member: each person chooses their own language without changing anything for anyone else. ISBN lookup draws on OpenLibrary. Many Greek-language titles are simply not in there — which is why entering a book by hand is an equal path, not a fallback. We write that down in advance, so you do not discover it while scanning five Greek books in a demonstration.

items.title: Can we set our own lending rules and our own fields?
items.body: Yes, to both. You set the loan period, whether renewals are allowed and how many, the daily fine and its cap, the replacement cost for lost items, how many copies a member may hold at once, and how many hours a copy waits on the pickup shelf. Beyond that you add fields of your own to six kinds of record — book, copy, member, loan, hold, fine — with ten field types, your own ordering, and labels in both English and Greek. A new field appears on the next form you open, with no request to us and no waiting. Fields are counted per kind of record, so Starter’s 3 means up to 18 in total.

items.title: What does not exist yet?
items.body: There is no public catalogue for readers and no member sign-in. There is no API and no integrations with other systems, no Z39.50 and no union catalogue, and the export does not produce MARC: we read MARC on the way in, we do not write it on the way out. There is no SMS, no phone notifications, no separate mobile app, no RFID and no self-service machines. You cannot yet define your own material types (for DVDs or board games) from inside the application. What is missing is missing; we do not charge for it as though it were there.

sections.heading: At the circulation desk, day to day

items.title: Can two or three people work at the same time?
items.body: Yes. Each person has their own staff seat and their own role, and you work simultaneously from different computers. The same copy cannot be lent twice: if two people put it through at the same moment, the second action stops with a message that the copy was just checked out from another station. The same applies to a hold that two people try to close together. How many people fit depends on the plan, from one staff seat on Starter to 30 on Institutional.

items.title: Does it work on a tablet or a phone at the desk?
items.body: Yes. The interface adapts to a small screen and installs onto the device’s home screen like an app, without going through an app store. It is not a separate mobile app: it is the same Libriant, through the browser. Scanning an ISBN or a barcode with the camera works wherever the browser supports it — today that means Chrome, Edge, the Android browsers and recent versions of Safari, while in Firefox you type the code in.

items.title: What happens if the internet connection drops?
items.body: Pages you had already opened stay usable with the last data the device saw, and the four desk actions — loan, return, renewal, marking an item lost — are recorded locally and sent as soon as the connection is back. Each action goes out with the same unique key it would have carried on a live connection, so a replay does not record the same return or the same fine twice. If an action has been waiting more than 18 hours it is not sent quietly: it is surfaced for you to redo by hand. Offline you cannot register a new title or a new member.

items.title: Do we need a barcode scanner and a label printer?
items.body: Not necessarily. An ordinary USB scanner types the barcode into whichever field you have open and works with no configuration; alternatively you scan with the camera, or type the code in. Libriant prints the labels itself: each label carries the library’s name, the title, the copy’s barcode and the shelf location, and comes out on whatever printer you already have. The same goes for the loan receipt. With the desktop app, which comes with the subscription plans, printing happens with no dialogue box, straight to the printer you nominate.

items.title: What can a Volunteer do, and what can they not?
items.body: There are three roles: Admin, Librarian, Volunteer. A Volunteer sees the catalogue, the members and the loans, but changes nothing: no lending, no recording a return, no adding a title or a member. It is the role for the people who help at the shelves and need to find things without being able to affect the data. A Librarian does all the day-to-day circulation, while an Admin additionally changes settings, adds staff and downloads the data export.

items.title: What happens to open loans when a member leaves?
items.body: A member is not archived while they are still holding a copy or have an active hold: the action stops and shows you how many loans and how many holds are outstanding, so no book is left behind on an archived record. An unpaid fine does not block archiving — it is shown, but collecting it is your decision. Once archived, the member stops counting towards your plan’s limit and their loan history stays. If they come back, you restore them.

sections.heading: Migrating from your current system
sections.intro: The steps in detail, together with what we need from you, are on the Migration page.

items.title: What can we come from, and what moves across?
items.body: You upload whatever you have: CSV, TSV, Excel (.xlsx), MARC21 (.mrc) or MARCXML — files that came out of ABEKT, out of Koha, out of a spreadsheet, or out of a card file that somebody typed up. Seven kinds of record move across: authors, books, copies, members, open loans, holds and fines, in that order, so that every loan finds its copy and its member. You are not starting from an empty desk: whatever is on loan today comes in on loan, with its due date. Which plans include bulk import is shown in the table on Plans and pricing; for the five founding libraries we do the move ourselves.

items.title: Will our Greek characters survive?
items.body: We also read files in Windows-1253, the old Greek code page, so your Greek does not come out mangled; detection is automatic and you convert nothing yourself. One case is not covered: older MARC files written in MARC-8. Their structure reads normally, but accented and special characters can come out wrong — in that case, export again from the old system in UTF-8, or in CSV. You will see it in the dry run, before anything is written.

items.title: How do we know the catalogue will not be wrecked?
items.body: Because nothing is written before you approve it. You match your file’s columns to Libriant’s fields and run a dry run first: you see how many rows will go in, how many carry an error and how many a warning, and you download a CSV of the problem rows so you can correct them in your own file and check again. For duplicates you choose the behaviour: skip, update the existing record, or raise an error so you can look at them one by one. And at every stage you can download your whole database, so you hold a copy of your own before and after.

sections.heading: Data, GDPR and who sees what
sections.intro: The Security and data protection page goes through all of it, and is written so that it can be forwarded as it stands to your IT department.

items.title: Where is our data held?
items.body: In the European Union, with daily backups and a copy kept off the server. Every library has its own separate database: you are not in shared tables with other libraries, and that isolation is checked by an automated test on every change to the code. This website has no cookies and no analytics — open the page source and you will see.

items.title: Which of you can see our data?
items.body: Nobody — not without a one-time code that you generate yourself. The access expires after four hours, you end it whenever you want, and you see every action we took written down, marked as “via Libriant support”. The code is handed over once, from you to us, and it is cancelled the moment you generate a new one.

items.title: Who is the controller for member data?
items.body: For your members’ data, you are the controller and we are the processor. Before you register your first member we sign a Data Processing Agreement that puts it in writing. Your members’ rights — access, rectification, erasure, portability — you serve from inside the application, and we provide the tools: search, export, correction, archiving.

items.title: What exactly does the activity log record?
items.body: It records who changed what in members, loans and library settings, with the before and after of each change, and it is there on every plan, including the free one. It does not currently cover changes to the catalogue: additions and corrections to titles are not logged, and we are not going to tell you that “every change” is recorded. Actions taken through support appear separately, marked as such.

sections.heading: Support, and the future of Libriant

items.title: And if you disappear?
items.body: Libriant is new and one person builds it. That is a real risk and we are not going to tell you otherwise. What we can do is remove the consequence: one button downloads your library’s whole database — as CSV, Excel, JSON, or a full PostgreSQL dump that restores as it stands — from the first day, on every plan, without asking us and with no notice period. The export does not include MARC; MARC is read on import, not produced on export. Keep a recent copy and the worst case is that you change system, not that you lose your catalogue.

items.title: Who answers us when something goes wrong?
items.body: The person who builds Libriant answers. There is no call centre and we are not going to pretend there is. You write to info@libriant.com and we answer every message within two working days; inside the application there is help with guidance for the everyday tasks, and for the five founding libraries we handle the migration ourselves. We do not offer a guaranteed response time or round-the-clock support: availability and support terms are agreed with you in writing before you start.

items.title: Can we see it before we decide?
items.body: There is no public demonstration instance, and we are not going to send you to one that does not exist. There are two routes: a short screen-sharing meeting, where we show whatever you want to see and answer your own questions, or the free Starter plan, which is a real system rather than a trial with a deadline. If what you want to see first is the migration, send us a sample of your file and we will show you what would go in.

items.title: Can we run it on our own servers?
items.body: Yes, by arrangement. The limits are set case by case and the pricing is agreed between us, because it depends on the size of the library and on what your own IT department takes on. Tell us what you need and we will answer in writing.

sections.heading: Something we have not answered here
body: Send your question to info@libriant.com. We answer every message within two working days, and when the answer matters to other libraries too, it gets added to this page.
Ask before you apply. You do not have to have decided in order to write to us, and we would rather have a question today than a misunderstanding in the third month.

title: Features — Libriant
metaDescription: What Libriant does today: catalogue, members, lending, holds, barcode scanning, a desktop app — and an honest list of what it does not do yet.
lede: This page describes what Libriant does today, in the language of the library rather than the language of software. At the end is the list of what it does not do yet — read that before you decide.

sections.heading: Catalogue
body: The catalogue has two levels: the title and its copies. The title holds the bibliographic detail — title, subtitle, authors in the order you enter them, publisher, year of publication, ISBN-13 and ISBN-10, edition, page count, language, classification or call number, description and cover. Each copy carries its own barcode, shelf location, circulation status and notes on its physical condition.
Plan limits count titles, not copies: ten copies of the same book are one title.

Type an ISBN and the book’s details are filled in for you. The source is OpenLibrary, and it is the only one. English-language publishing is reasonably well covered there; Greek-language titles are often absent — which is why entering a record by hand is an equal path through the software and not a fallback.
Search ignores accents and letter case, in either alphabet: “cafe” finds “Café”, “καβαφης” finds “Καβάφη”. It looks at title, subtitle, authors, publisher, year and ISBN at the same time.
A title that is no longer in circulation is archived rather than deleted. It leaves the working lists, it stops counting towards your plan limit, and everything recorded against it stays.

sections.heading: Members
body: Every member is given a member number. If you do not supply one, it is generated in the form M-2026-0001. The record holds full name, email, phone, date of birth, address, and notes that your staff can see and the member cannot.

A member is active, suspended or archived. A member who is not active cannot be lent to and cannot have a hold placed for them. An archived member stops counting towards your plan limit, while their loan history stays.
Member search looks at full name, email, phone and city, again ignoring accents and case. The member number is matched exactly: scan it from the card and the record opens.

sections.heading: Lending
sections.intro: The daily flow at the circulation desk. Every action is performed on a specific copy, never on the title.

items.title: Loan
items.body: You choose a member and a copy. The due date is calculated from the loan period your library has set. If the member has reached their limit of active loans, the checkout stops there with a clear message.

items.title: Return
items.body: You record the return and note whether the copy came back in good condition or damaged. If there is a hold queue for the title, the copy is set aside for the next member straight away instead of going back to the shelf.

items.title: Renewal
items.body: If your library allows renewals, the loan is extended up to the number of times you set. Renewal stops when another member is waiting in the hold queue for the same title.

items.title: Overdues and fines
items.body: If you have fines switched on, the amount grows automatically for every day the copy stays overdue, up to the ceiling you set per loan. See below for what is not covered yet around collecting them.

items.title: Lost copy
items.body: You mark the loan as lost. The copy leaves circulation and, if you have enabled it, a replacement cost is recorded against the member.

sections.heading: Holds and the hold queue
body: Holds are placed by staff. There is no screen on which a member places a hold for themselves — the librarian opens it on their behalf, at the desk or over the phone.

The hold queue keeps its order of priority. If a copy is available at the moment the hold is placed, the hold goes straight to ready for pickup and that copy is set aside. Otherwise it joins the queue with its position.

As soon as a copy is returned, the first person in the queue is promoted automatically to ready for pickup, and the pickup window you have set — in hours — begins. If the window passes, the hold expires, the copy is released and the next person is promoted.
The same member cannot hold the same title twice, and cannot place a hold on a book they already have on loan. Holds are not part of the free plan.

sections.heading: Library policy
sections.intro: Circulation rules are not fixed in Libriant. You set them yourself, under Settings → Library policy & features, without asking us.
rows: Loan period
How many days a loan runs. The due date is calculated from this.
Renewals
Whether they are allowed, and how many times the same loan can be renewed.
Active loans per member
How many copies a member may hold at once. Zero means no limit.
Overdue fines
Whether they are charged, how much per day, and the maximum per loan.
Lost-item fees
Whether a replacement cost is recorded, and what the default amount is.
Holds
Whether you use holds, and how many hours a copy waits on the pickup shelf.
Notifications
Which of the three notices are switched on, and how many days before the due date the reminder goes out.
Currency
The currency in which fines and fees are expressed.
sections.footnote: Changes take effect from the moment you save. Loans already open keep the due date that was calculated when they were issued.

sections.heading: Your own fields
body: No library fits a ready-made form. You add custom fields to six kinds of record: book, copy, member, loan, hold and fine.

There are ten field types: short text, long text, number, yes/no, date, date and time, pick one, pick many, link and email. Each field takes a label in both Greek and English, is marked required or optional, and is dragged into the order you want.

Beside the list is a live preview of the form your staff will fill in. Changes take effect the next time a form loads: the records you already have are untouched, there is nothing to wait for, and nothing has to be requested from us.

A field you no longer need is archived rather than deleted, and older records keep their values. Custom fields are counted per kind of record, not in total — so your plan’s limit applies six times over.

sections.heading: Barcode scanning, mobile and offline
body: At checkout, at return and when cataloguing a book you can scan instead of typing: the ISBN from the back cover, a copy barcode, a membership card. Scanning uses the device’s own camera, with no extra hardware.

It rests, though, on a browser capability that not every browser has. It works in Chrome, Edge, Android and recent versions of Safari; it does not work in Firefox; and it needs a secure connection and permission for the camera. Where it is not supported the scan button does not appear at all and the number is typed, as it always was. Nothing in the workflow depends on scanning.

Libriant installs on a phone or tablet as an app, from the browser itself. In practice that means working between the shelves with the device in your hand, instead of notes that are typed up again afterwards.

When the connection drops, the four desk actions — checkout, return, renewal and marking a copy lost — queue up inside the device and are sent as soon as the network returns. Each action carries a key of its own, so that sending it twice does not become two loans.
Pages you have looked at recently are shown offline as well, from the device’s local storage. On sign-out that storage is cleared, so a shared machine does not show the previous person’s data.

sections.heading: Desktop app
body: There is also a desktop app, for Windows, macOS and Linux. It is the same application in a window of its own, with the things a browser is not permitted to do.

The most important of those is silent printing. The checkout receipt and the copy label go straight to the printer, without a print dialogue opening at every loan. The label prints your library’s name, the title, the copy’s barcode in Code 128, and the shelf location.

The app updates itself, remembers the size and position of its window, asks for camera permission so that you can scan from the desk, and when the server does not answer it shows a recovery screen rather than a blank window.
The desktop app comes with the plans that carry a subscription. It is not part of the free plan.

sections.heading: Email notifications
body: Libriant has three ready-made messages to your members: a reminder that a due date is approaching, a notice that a loan is overdue, and a notice that a hold is ready for pickup.

All three are off to begin with. You switch them on one at a time, and the members contacted are those with an email address on file. No library should start sending messages to its members because it opened an account.
The wording of each notice is yours: there is a default text and you replace it from the settings. Messages are written in your library’s own language.

Today no email leaves for a member. No mail sender has been configured yet, so the switches, the wording and the regular sweep of the loans all exist, but nothing goes out. We will write it here when that changes.
Email notifications are not part of the free plan.

sections.heading: Staff and accountability
sections.intro: Not everyone on your staff needs the same rights. There are three roles, and changes to members, loans and settings are recorded with the value before and after.

items.title: Admin
items.body: Settings, library policy, staff, the data model, import and export. The account that created the library holds these rights.

items.title: Librarian
items.body: The daily work: catalogue, members, loans, holds. No access to the library’s settings.

items.title: Volunteer
items.body: Sees everything, changes nothing. A role for helpers who do not carry responsibility for the data.

items.title: Activity log
items.body: Who, when, what — with the value before and after. It covers creating, updating, changing the status of and archiving a member, checkout, return, renewal and marking lost, and every change of settings. Changes to the catalogue are not recorded yet.

items.title: Staff seats
items.body: A new account is created with a username and a temporary password, which you hand to the person themselves; at their first sign-in they set their own name and password. An account that is deactivated stops counting towards your plan’s limit.

items.title: Support access
items.body: None of us sees your data without a one-time code that you generate. The access expires after four hours, you end it whenever you want, and every action we take appears in the activity log marked “via Libriant support”.

sections.footnote: The activity log is opened by Admins. It is a tool for oversight, not for daily work.

sections.heading: Greek and English
body: Every screen exists in both languages. Not a translation that arrived afterwards, but two texts of equal standing from the start — the same is true of the help articles inside the application.
The language is set by the page’s address: /en/ for English, /el/ for Greek. Two people at the same desk can work in different languages, with nothing changing for the library.

The library’s default language is set at signup, taken from the language the signup is made in, and messages to members are written in it. Your own fields take a label in both languages, so that one form reads in either.

If you teach in English inside Greece, run a foreign-language college, keep a special library inside an organisation, or work in Cyprus, this is the part that decides whether a system is usable at your desk. Staff who prefer English and staff who prefer Greek are reading the same records.

sections.heading: Import and export
body: You upload what you have — CSV, TSV, an Excel sheet, MARC21 or MARCXML — match your columns to Libriant’s fields, and run a dry run first. The dry run tells you how many rows will go in, which carry an error and which a warning, and gives you a CSV of the rows that need attention. All of that before anything is written.
Seven kinds of record come across: authors, books, copies, members, loans, holds and fines. Alongside the catalogue, that is, the open loans and the outstanding holds arrive too.
We also read files in Windows-1253, the legacy Greek code page, so that Greek text does not arrive broken. On duplicates you decide: skip, update the existing record, or report an error.

Bulk import is included in every plan that carries a subscription. It is not part of the free Starter plan — there, if you have a file to bring over, we run the migration ourselves with a support code that you generate. The steps, the limits and the traps — MARC-8, Greek Excel files with a semicolon instead of a comma — are on the [Migration](/en/migration) page.

Export, by contrast, is on every plan including the free one, without asking us and without giving anyone notice. You download your library’s whole database in four formats: CSV in a zip archive, JSON, Excel, or a full PostgreSQL dump that restores as it stands. MARC we read on the way in; we do not produce it on the way out.

sections.heading: What it does not do yet
sections.intro: This list is here on purpose. We would rather you read it now than meet it in your third month. Every line is a fact with its reason.

items.title: A public catalogue for readers (OPAC)
items.body: There is none. Libriant today is the staff’s tool, and there is no screen a reader ever sees. If what you need is for the public to find your collection in a national catalogue, openABEKT is the right answer for a library in Greece, and we will tell you so plainly. Libriant solves the internal problem: who has which book, and when it comes back.

items.title: Accounts for members
items.body: Members do not sign in anywhere. They cannot see what they have borrowed, they cannot renew, they cannot place holds. Every hold goes through a librarian.

items.title: Access for other systems
items.body: There is no interface for other software to talk to Libriant, and no ready-made integrations. The way your data leaves is the export, which you have always and on every plan.

items.title: Z39.50, union catalogues, copy cataloguing
items.body: Not supported. You cannot pull a finished bibliographic record from another library, nor send yours to a union catalogue.

items.title: MARC export
items.body: MARC comes in; it does not go out. The export formats are CSV, JSON, Excel and a full PostgreSQL dump. If leaving a system depends on MARC on the way out, know it from now.

items.title: Greek bibliographic sources for ISBN
items.body: ISBN lookup draws on OpenLibrary alone. There is no connection to the National Library or to a Greek publishing database. Scan five Greek books and three may well come back empty — which is why entering a record by hand is an equal path and not a fallback.

items.title: Email notifications that go out today
items.body: The three notices exist, with their wording, their switches and a regular sweep of the loans, but no mail sender has been configured yet — so no message reaches a member. We do not charge for something that is not being sent, and we will update this page when it changes.

items.title: SMS and phone notifications
items.body: There are none. Towards members there is one channel, email — and that one with the limitation on the line above.

items.title: A mobile app in the App Store or Play Store
items.body: There is none. Libriant installs on a phone from the browser and behaves like an app, but it is not a store app. The desktop app, by contrast, is a real application that you download and install.

items.title: Separate material types (DVDs, board games, archival material)
items.body: Every record in the catalogue is a book. You cannot define a material type of your own with screens of its own. If your holdings are mixed, the practical route today is a field of your own — “material type” — on the record.

items.title: Paying and writing off a fine
items.body: Fines are calculated automatically and the outstanding amount shows on the member’s record. There is no screen yet on which to record that a fine was paid or written off. If you collect fines, recording the payment happens outside Libriant for now.

items.title: Recording changes to the catalogue
items.body: The activity log covers members, loans and settings. Adding, correcting or archiving a title is not recorded yet, so do not rely on it for cataloguing oversight.

items.title: Statistics and ready-made reports
items.body: The home screen shows counters: titles, members, active loans, overdues, holds waiting. There is no reports page and no ready-made charts. For analysis you download your data and work on it in Excel.

items.title: Acquisitions and serials
items.body: There is no management of orders for new material and no tracking of issues. Libriant covers the catalogue, members and circulation.

items.title: RFID, self-service kiosks, online fine payment
items.body: Not supported. Libriant assumes one desk, a camera or a barcode scanner, and a person.

sections.heading: See it with your own data
body: There is no public trial version and we will not send you to one that does not exist. What there is, is a short meeting over a shared screen, where we show you what you have read above and answer whatever was not covered here.
If you want to see how your own catalogue comes across, send us a sample of your file. A few dozen rows are enough.
